drivers.evidence: Historical noise-adjusted effect: x0.8 (2 past occurrences, 2024-06-10: x0.55, 2025-06-09: x0.6)

drivers.name: 10% off promotion (deeper than prior 10% off)
drivers.evidence: Price cut 9.9% vs regular; past 10% off promotions had noise-adjusted x1.0; deeper discount than prior 10% off, but not as deep as 25% off (x1.22), so moderate uplift

adjustment.analysis: Baseline median is 13.4. Father's Day historically lowers sales (noise-adjusted x0.8), and this week's 10% promotion is similar to past 10% off events that averaged x1.0 (noise-adjusted). However, the 25% off promotion in 2026-04-20 had a larger lift (x1.22), and the price is now 4.53 (9.9% below regular), deeper than previous 10% off. The classical model underweights this depth and overweights the holiday effect. Adjust upward for the deeper discount, but shrink toward 1.0 due to limited evidence. The holiday effect is real but small. No pantry-loading signal from recent weeks.

brief:
PRODUCT: Hot Cocoa Mix | category Grocery | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-06-15 to 2026-06-21 (next week)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: Holiday: Father's Day (Sun); Promotion: 10% off
  shelf price: 4.53 (-9.9% vs regular price 5.03)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 13.4 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 26.6 | 10%-90%: 0.9 - 25.6

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-53% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
